legend: Pep is late for his competitive programming lecture. His building has n+1$$$n + 1$$$ floors, and he lives on the floor n+1$$$n + 1$$$. To go to college, he calls the elevator to his floor. Since he's superstitious, if the elevator stops on more than one floor besides the one it was on when he called and his floor, n+1$$$n + 1$$$, he believes the day will be bad and goes back to bed.

While the elevator is moving, each floor i$$$i$$$ has a probability pi$$$p_i$$$ that the neighbor on floor i$$$i$$$ will call the elevator at that moment, causing it to stop. Fortunately for Pep, his neighbors are not obsessed with constantly calling the elevator, that is, pi<100%$$$p_i  \lt  100\%$$$ for 1≤i≤n$$$1 \le i \le n$$$.

During the college semester, his neighbors may move out, and new neighbors may arrive, changing the probability pi$$$p_i$$$ of floor i$$$i$$$. Pep would also like to make queries to determine the probability of going to class, given that the elevator would be on floor x$$$x$$$ when he calls it.
input: The first line consists of two integers n$$$n$$$ (3≤n≤2⋅105)$$$(3\le n \le 2\cdot 10^5)$$$ and q$$$q$$$ (1≤q≤2⋅105)$$$(1\le q \le 2\cdot 10^5)$$$.

The second line consists of n$$$n$$$ integers pi$$$p_i$$$ (0≤pi<100)$$$(0 \le p_i  \lt  100)$$$, representing the probability (in percentage) that the elevator will stop on floor i$$$i$$$ while in motion.
The next q$$$q$$$ lines correspond to queries of two types:
∙$$$\bullet$$$ 1$$$1$$$ x$$$x$$$ p$$$p$$$: Change the probability of floor x$$$x$$$, updating px$$$p_x$$$ to p$$$p$$$.
∙$$$\bullet$$$ 2$$$2$$$ x$$$x$$$: Answer with the probability that Pep will go to class, given that the elevator is on floor x$$$x$$$ when he calls it.
output: For each query of type 2$$$2$$$, output a line with the queried probability. We can prove that this probability can be expressed as an irreducible fraction pq$$$\frac{p}{q}$$$. Print p⋅q−1$$$p \cdot q^{-1}$$$ modulo (109+7)$$$(10^9 + 7)$$$.
note: The probability of not stopping on floors 2$$$2$$$ and 3$$$3$$$ is 14$$$\frac{1}{4}$$$.
The probability of stopping only on floor 2$$$2$$$ is 14$$$\frac{1}{4}$$$.
The probability of stopping only on floor 3$$$3$$$ is 14$$$\frac{1}{4}$$$.
